paragraphs.text: Americans are living longer these days, long enough to become vehicular terrors behind the wheel in their eighties and nineties, and they’re injuring themselves and others at unprecedented rates. David Howard, with additional reporting from Lloyd Alter, does the math and suggests that simply taking a senior’s licence away is not the answer; America is car-centric and many seniors need to drive in order to grocery shop, attend health appointments, and to meet their social needs. Could autonomous vehicles provide the balance we need between safety and independence?

Already visible on the technological horizon, of course, are self-driving cars, which carry the potential to obviate many of the limitations older drivers face. Mark Needham (not his real name) lives on the fringes of Charlottesville, Virgina. He is 82 and still active: He practices yoga at a local health club, engages in a glassblowing hobby, and dabbles with technology. He and his wife, 80, have lived in the same subdivision for 40 years, and while she’s wrestling with several health issues and is ready to move into a retirement facility, he’s adamantly opposed to it. “My wife is more inclined to being taken care of,” Needham says.“I’m more inclined to be doing stuff.”

Part of what allows him to maintain his independence: a Tesla that over his two-plus years of ownership has morphed, via a steady stream of software updates, into a largely autonomous vehicle. (Many reviewers and experts still cite the need for improvement with tasks like changing speeds and parking before use becomes widespread.) “It drives better than I drove 30 or 40 years ago,” he says.
